10:Belay provides four constructs: `agent`, `skill`, `command`, and `instruction`.
11-Here we'll talk about their functional purpose, and in a later section we'll
12-discuss the roles they play and how to structure them when building out a
13-complex application.
14-
15-## Skill
16-
17:A skill is a triggerable set of instructions that the agent can load to perform
18-specific things. In a large application, it is conceivable to have tens to even
19-several hundred skills that target specific aspects of the application.
20-
21-Rather than loading all skills into the active context, agentic platforms will
22-use the description to determine when the skill is needed. That's why Belay
23-makes `useWhen` a mandatory property of a skill anchor:
24-
25-```piton
26-abstract anchor Skill as skill:
27-    description:: string
28-    prompt:: string
29-    useWhen:: string
30-```
31-
32-A skill will compile into the correct skill directory and format for whichever
33-adapters are configured in the project.
34-
35-```markdown
36----
37-name: { anchor name }
38-description: { description } Use when { useWhen }
39----
40-
41-{prompt}
42-{string serialized version of the skill}
--
48-Additional properties and and types and string interpolations will be rendered
49-according to the [serialization rules](/belay/serialization).
50-
51:## Instruction
52-
53:Instructions are a special construct. They look like:
54-
55-```piton
56:abstract anchor Instruction as instruction:
57-    description:: string
58-    prompt:: string
59-```
60-
61-Which at first doesn't look very unique at all. However, it's the way they're
62-compiled that carries a lot of the weight. It'll end up making a lot more sense
63-when we start talking about best practices and strategies for structuring a
64-specification.
65-
66:The purpose of an instruction is primarily to be compiled into the correct
67-`codeRoot` directory as the equivalent of an `AGENTS.md` file according to what
68-each adapter/agentic platform supports. In Belay, we have a concept of a
69-`codeRoot` directory, as well as a `shapeRoot` directory; `shapeRoot` is
70-supposed to be an approximate mirror of the generated `codeRoot` structure. So
71-for example, if you have a `codeRoot` that looks like:
72-
73-<FileTree>
74-- src
75-    - components
76-        - button
77-        - index.tsx
78-    - input
79-        - index.tsx
80-</FileTree>
81-
82-The expectation is that your `shapeRoot` will mirror this structure:
83-
84-<FileTree>
85-- spec
86-    - shape
87-        - components
88-            - button
89-                - Button.pi
90-            - input
91-                - Input.pi
--
110-</FileTree>
111-
112-If the `codeRoot` structure does not match the `shapeRoot` structure, the
113:instructions will be concatenated to the next level up that does match,
114-terminating at a `codeRoot/AGENTS.md` file.
115-
116-<FileTree>
117-- spec
118-    - shape
119-        - components
120-            - **nonexistentComponent**
121-                - Component.pi
122-</FileTree>
123-
124-goes into
125-
126-<FileTree>
127-- src
128-    - components
129-        - **AGENTS.md**
130-</FileTree>
131-
132:In addition to this, all instructions contained under `shapeRoot` will be
133-compiled into the agent directory (`.claude` for example) under the
134-`reference/shape` directory maintaining their relative structure.
135-
136-Additional properties and and types and string interpolations will be rendered
137-according to the [serialization rules](/belay/serialization).
138-
139-### Special `__BELAY_SHAPE__` Variable
140-
141-Belay exports a special `__BELAY_SHAPE__` variable that contains the compiled
142-shape root directory -- what we previously referenced in an example as
143-`.claude/reference/shape`.
144-
145-We can import that to write specific skills:
146-
147-```piton
148-use @piton/belay
149-
150-from @piton/belay import __BELAY_SHAPE__
151-
152-// Intentionally minimal just for the sake of example
153-export skill BuildSpec:
154-    description: Build what's in the specification
155-    useWhen: You're about to ${self.description}
156-    prompt:
157-        Build following the structure outlined in ${__BELAY_SHAPE__}
use @piton/config
use @piton/belay

from @piton/belay import ClaudeAdapter

export piton-config Config:
    root: ./spec
    entry: ./spec/index.pi

    frameworks:
        - {BelayFrameworkConfig}

belay-config BelayFrameworkConfig:
    // The codebase you are describing. Point this at the source you already
    // have. This config also declares a shapeRoot, which mirrors codeRoot
    // directory for directory — that is what makes an instruction compile
    // next to the code it describes.
    codeRoot: ./src/
    shapeRoot: ./spec/shape/

    adapters:
        - {ClaudeAdapter}

I added a small New Instruction button to the Spec tab's Components group. It creates the instruction file under the shape root (`spec/shape` here), not the spec root. You pick a folder or file under `src`, name the instruction, and write it yourself in the same editor used for project files, before anything is written to disk. All 209 tests pass (1 ignored), the build has no warnings, and `piton check`, `piton build check` and `piton build` pass. I haven't checked the language server (LSP) features in this panel: tests don't run it, and I haven't tried the panel on screen.

**Where it writes** (your call): Belay's docs say an instruction only compiles next to the code it describes when it sits under `shapeRoot`, which mirrors `codeRoot` folder for folder. Under the plain spec root, Belay can't match it to that code. So:
- `src/ribbon/spec_tab.rs` becomes `spec/shape/ribbon/SpecTab.pi`.
- The folder `src/ribbon/` becomes `spec/shape/ribbon/Ribbon.pi`.
- A project with no `shapeRoot` falls back to the spec root, and the panel says so.

If you really do want the spec root, it's a one-line change.

**How it works** (`src/new_instruction.rs`):
1. **Choose:** a searchable Code dropdown of every folder and file under the code root, respecting `.gitignore`.
   - **Name:** filled in from your choice as you pick (e.g. `spec_tab.rs` gives `SpecTab`) until you edit it.
   - **Target note:** shows the file that will be written.
   - **Continue:** stays disabled until a name is valid and the target file doesn't already exist.
2. **Write:** the panel shows the new file in the editor, filled in with `use @piton/belay`, an `export instruction SpecTab:` anchor, its description ("Instructions for src/ribbon/spec_tab.rs"), and a placeholder prompt line with the cursor on it. There's no AI step.
3. **Save and close:** saving writes the file and creates any missing folders. Closing the editor, or the panel any other way, asks first if there are unsaved changes. Once saved and closed, the file opens beside the chat.

**Editor reuse:** the panel uses the existing file editor itself, so it gets everything that editor does, including language support for `.pi` files. The one addition is that it can now show a file that isn't on disk yet.

**Spec:**
- **New Instruction scope:** new, in `spec/scope/spec-components/`, referencing the Editor and LSP scopes.
- **Spec tab:** has the new slim command.
- **Components scope:** lists the new command and notes it has no description or skill.
- **Editor scope:** describes files not yet on disk.
- **Project Locations scope:** now names the shape location.

**Tests:**
- **Unit tests:** cover name generation, the path mirroring (with and without `shapeRoot`), and the folder/file listing. They also check that the starting template passes `piton check` in a real Belay project.
- **UI test:** runs the full flow:
  - the button sits in the stack;
  - it picks `src/ribbon/spec_tab.rs` and checks the target path;
  - Continue opens the editor with nothing written yet;
  - closing the panel with unsaved changes asks first;
  - saving writes the file;
  - closing the editor opens it beside the chat.
